{{short description|Problem solving strategy}}

'''Symmetry in problem solving''' is one of the general methods used in mathematics and science to solve problems. Problem solving plays a large part in the teaching of mathematics, science and engineering. The use of symmetry as one of a number of problem solving strategies ([[heuristic]]s) was first stated in 1945 by [[George Pólya]] in his book ''[[How to solve it]]''.

==Usage==
[[File:Hexagon and 6 equilateral triangles.svg|thumb|upright=0.9|alt=Diagram showing a hexagon divided into 6 equilateral triangles|A hexagon divided symmetrically into 6 equilateral triangles to assist in calculating its area]]
Symmetry can be used in a variety of ways to assist in problem solving.

* Visualisation: by visualising the problem sometimes symmetry is revealed which simplifies finding a solution. Visualisation can be done by rearranging the problem expression into a more symmetric form, or by drawing a picture of the problem which reveals hidden symmetrical structure. Diagramming can be used to provide insight into the structure of a problem which may be obscured by its written formulation.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Vale |first1=Isabel |last2=Pimentel |first2=Teresa |last3=Barbosa |first3=Ana |chapter=The Power of Seeing in Problem Solving and Creativity: An Issue Under Discussion |title=Broadening the Scope of Research on Mathematical Problem Solving |date=2018 |pages=243–272 |editor-last1=Amado |editor-first1=Nélia |editor-last2=Carreira |editor-first2=Susana |editor-last3=Jones |editor-first3=Keith |isbn=978-3-319-99861-9 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-99861-9_11}}</ref>
* Arguing "by symmetry": using a symmetry argument often clarifies a problem, leading to a quicker solution. For example, algebraic symmetry allows the permutation of the variables in an equation without changing it.<ref name=Leikin/>{{rp|page=806}}<ref name=Discovery/>{{rp|page=vol. 1, p. 153}}
* Simplification: algebraic expressions and equations often benefit from simplification using symmetry. An example is the use of substitutions in expressions. Another example is switching from Cartesian coordinates to polar, cylindrical, or spherical coordinates to better suit the problem.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Krantz |first1=Steven G. |title=An episodic history of mathematics: mathematical culture through problem solving |date=2010 |publisher=Mathematical Association of America |location=Washington, DC |isbn=978-0883857663 |page=151}}</ref>
* Inheritance: if the problem has symmetry, the solution will often inherit that symmetry.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Waterhouse |first1=William C. |title=Do Symmetric Problems Have Symmetric Solutions? |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |date=June 1983 |volume=90 |issue=6 |pages=378–387 |doi=10.1080/00029890.1983.11971235}}</ref>
* Eliminating impossible solutions: symmetry can be used to rule out potential solutions that would contradict the structure of the problem.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Averbach |first1=Bonnie |last2=Chein |first2=Orin |title=Problem solving through recreational mathematics |date=2000 |publisher=Dover |location=Mineola (N.Y.) |isbn=0-486-40917-1 |pages=234–240 |url=https://archive.org/details/Problem.Solving.Through.Recreational.Mathematics/page/n247/mode/2up |access-date=17 April 2026}}</ref>
* Breaking down the problem: if the problem has a symmetrical structure it may be sufficient to solve only part of it, and then the full solution can follow by extension.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ording |first1=Philip |title=[[99 Variations on a Proof]] |date=2019 |publisher=Princeton University Press |location=Princeton |isbn=978-0-691-15883-9 |page=52}}</ref> For example, to calculate the area of a regular hexagon, divide it into equilateral triangles, calculate the area of a triangle using the formula half base times height by applying the [[Pythagorean theorem]], and then multiply by 6. Pólya believed that symmetry assisted in problem solving by reducing and ordering the observable facts.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Pólya |first1=George |title=Mathematics and plausible reasoning vol. I Induction and analogy in mathematics |date=1954 |publisher=Princeton University Press |page=88}}</ref>

==Examples==
===Mathematics===
[[File:Gauss Summation (1+2+...+99+100).svg|thumb|upright=0.9|alt=Diagram of Gauss summation of the first 100 integers|Using symmetry to sum the first 100 integers (traditionally attributed to [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]])]]
The [[Sum of integers|sum of the integers]] from 1 to 100 can be calculated by pairing the outer two integers (1+100=101), the next two integers (2+99=101) and continuing the process to the two inmost integers (50+51=101). The process yields 50 pairs each with a sum of 101, totalling 5,050. The solution of the problem is traditionally attributed to [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Moore-Russo |first1=Deborah |last2=Demler |first2=Erica L. |editor1-last=Amado |editor1-first=Nélia |editor2-last=Carreira |editor2-first=Susana |editor3-last=Jones |editor3-first=Keith |title=Broadening the Scope of Research on Mathematical Problem Solving: A Focus on Technology, Creativity and Affect |date=2018 |publisher=Springer International Publishing : Imprint: Springer |location=Cham |isbn=978-3-319-99861-9 |page=327 |chapter=Linking Mathematical Creativity to Problem Solving: Views from the Field |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-99861-9_14}}</ref> The line of integers has reflection symmetry at its midpoint; the solver can think of folding at the line of reflection to bring each of the pairs together.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hayes |first1=Brian |title=Gauss's Day of Reckoning |journal=American Scientist |date=2006 |volume=94 |issue=3 |pages=200–205 |doi=10.1511/2006.59.200 |jstor=27858762 |url-status=live |url=https://www.americanscientist.org/article/gausss-day-of-reckoning |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402141244/http://www.americanscientist.org/issues/pub/gausss-day-of-reckoning/1 |archive-date=2 April 2015 |access-date=14 April 2026|url-access=subscription }}</ref>{{rp|page=204}}

[[File:Geometric symmetry problem example.svg|thumb|upright=0.9|alt=Geometric diagram of a square inscribed in a circle inscribed in a larger square|Problem: What is the area of a square inscribed in a circle, which itself is inscribed in a larger square? Solution: The small square has half the area of the large square.]]
It is not immediately obvious what is the area of a small square inscribed in a circle, which itself is inscribed in a large square. However, by rotating the small square by 90° and then drawing the two diagonals of the small square, it becomes clear that the small square is composed of 4 identical triangles (red) and the large square of 8 identical triangles (blue and red), and therefore the small square has half the area of the large square. The use of the rotation symmetry operation simplifies finding the solution.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Zeitz |first1=Paul |title=The art and craft of problem solving |date=2017 |publisher=Wiley |location=Hoboken, NJ |isbn=978-1-119-23990-1 |pages=59–70 |chapter=Symmetry |edition=Third}}</ref>{{rp|page=60}}

The mathematical theory of symmetry, that is [[group theory]], is now widely recognised for its problem-solving utility.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hamermesh |first1=M. |title=Group theory and its application to physical problems |date=1989 |orig-date=1962 |publisher=Dover Publications |location=New York |isbn=978-0486661810 |url=https://archive.org/details/grouptheoryitsap0000hame_x9g8  |url-access=registration |access-date=14 April 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chester |first1=Marvin |title=Is symmetry identity? |journal=International Studies in the Philosophy of Science |date=July 2002 |volume=16 |issue=2 |pages=111–124 |doi=10.1080/02698590220145061|arxiv=1202.0292 }}</ref>{{rp|page=112}} The field of solutions of [[differential equations]] is largely driven by symmetry considerations.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stephani |first1=Hans |last2=MacCallum |first2=M. A. H. |title=Differential equations: their solution using symmetries |date=1989 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge [England]; New York |isbn=0-521-35531-1}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rosenhaus |first1=V. |last2=Shankar |first2=Ravi |last3=Squellati |first3=Cody |title=Symmetries and Separation of Variables |journal=Journal of Nonlinear Mathematical Physics |date=8 August 2024 |volume=31 |issue=1 |doi=10.1007/s44198-024-00218-9|doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Physics===
Symmetry is ubiquitous in solving problems in modern physics;<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Antoine |first1=Jean-Pierre |title=Group Theory: Mathematical Expression of Symmetry in Physics |journal=Symmetry |date=26 July 2021 |volume=13 |issue=8 |pages=1354–1364 |doi=10.3390/sym13081354 |doi-access=free|hdl=2078.1/249856 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> for example, [[Albert Einstein]] used symmetry arguments in his 1905 paper ''On the electrodynamics of moving bodies'' in developing his [[special theory of relativity]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Einstein |first1=A. |title=On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies |journal=Special Theory of Relativity |date=1970 |pages=187–218 |doi=10.1016/b978-0-08-006995-1.50014-4}}</ref> Conservation theorems are closely connected with the symmetry properties of physical systems ([[Noether's theorem]]).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Goldstein |first1=Herbert |last2=Poole |first2=Charles P. |last3=Safko |first3=John L. |title=Classical mechanics |date=2002 |publisher=Addison-Wesley |pages=55–61,589–598 |isbn=978-81-317-5891-5}}</ref> [[Group theory]] and [[Lie algebras]] are extensively used in solving problems in [[quantum mechanics]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rowe |first1=D. J. |last2=Carvalho |first2=M. J. |last3=Repka |first3=J. |title=Dual pairing of symmetry and dynamical groups in physics |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |date=11 May 2012 |volume=84 |issue=2 |pages=711–757 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.84.711|arxiv=1207.0148 }}</ref> and in many other areas of physics.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cantwell |first1=Brian |title=Introduction to symmetry analysis |date=2002 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge, UK; New York |isbn=978-052177183-2 |url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontosy0000cant |access-date=17 April 2026 |url-access=registration}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Ludwig |first1=Wolfgang |last2=Falter |first2=C. |title=Symmetries in Physics: Group Theory Applied to Physical Problems |date=1988 |publisher=Springer |location=Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-642-97031-3}}</ref>

===Chemistry===
Symmetry considerations are frequently used in chemistry to solve problems.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Fackler |first1=John P. |title=Symmetry in chemical theory: application of group theoretical techniques to the solution of chemical problems |date=1973 |publisher=Dowden, Hutchinson & Ross |location=Stroudsburg, PA |isbn=0-87933-018-X |url=https://archive.org/details/symmetryinchemic0000fack |access-date=17 April 2026 |url-access=registration}}</ref> Symmetry is used in [[Structural chemistry|structural determinations]], for the prediction of [[molecular electronic transition]]s, and in the interpretation of [[Reactivity (chemistry)|chemical reactivity]], and [[Crystallography|crystallographic]] and [[Spectroscopy|spectroscopic]] data. Symmetry can also be used in [[organic synthesis]] and [[catalysis]] as a means to increase the [[stereoselectivity]] of chemical reactions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Moberg |first1=Christina |title=Symmetry as a Tool for Solving Chemical Problems |journal=Bulletin of the Chemical Society of Japan |date=15 February 2021 |volume=94 |issue=2 |pages=558–564 |doi=10.1246/bcsj.20200338}}</ref> The mechanism of [[pericyclic reaction]]s can be predicted by the application of the [[Woodward–Hoffmann rules]] (the conservation of orbital symmetry) which are based on the symmetries of [[molecular orbital]]s.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lehr |first1=Roland E. |last2=Marchand |first2=Alan P. |title=Orbital symmetry: a problem-solving approach |date=1972 |publisher=Academic Press |location=New York |isbn=0-12-441156-8 |url=https://archive.org/details/orbitalsymmetryp0000lehr |access-date=16 April 2026 |url-access=registration}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Kumar |first1=Sunil |last2=Kumar |first2=Vinod |last3=Singh |first3=S. P. |title=Pericyclic reactions: a mechanistic and problem-solving approach |date=2016 |publisher=Academic Press is an imprint of Elsevier |location=London, UK; San Diego, CA, USA |isbn=978-0-12-803640-2}}</ref>

==Education==
Secondary school classroom and professional development studies have shown that symmetry is one of the effective strategies for mathematical problem solving, and aids students in pattern recognition, algebraic manipulation, and geometric reasoning.<ref name=Leikin>{{cite journal |last1=Leikin |first1=Roza |last2=Berman |first2=Abraham |last3=Zaslavsky |first3=Orit |title=Applications of symmetry to problem solving |journal=International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology |date=November 2000 |volume=31 |issue=6 |pages=799–809 |doi=10.1080/00207390050203315}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Steiner |first1=Hans-Georg |title=The Teaching of Geometry at the Pre-College Level: Proceedings of the Second CSMP International Conference |date=1971 |publisher=Springer Netherlands |location=Dordrecht |isbn=978-94-017-5896-3}}</ref> Symmetry is also useful to students in solving physics problems.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Frodyma |first1=Marc |last2=Rosas |first2=Sandy |title=Using Symmetry and Invariance to Solve Problems in Elementary Physics |journal=The Physics Teacher |date=1 October 2019 |volume=57 |issue=7 |pages=475–477 |doi=10.1119/1.5126828}}</ref> National mathematics standards and curricula normally incorporate goals for problem solving and for understanding and using symmetry, for example the standards in the USA.<ref>{{cite web |title=Mathematics Standards |url=https://www.thecorestandards.org/Math/ |website=Common Core State Standards |access-date=17 April 2026}}</ref>{{rp|Grade 4, p. 27}}

==History==
In modern times, the use of symmetry to solve geometrical problems is common, as expressed by the phrase "... (and so) by symmetry ...",<ref>{{cite web |last1=Shelomovskii |first1=Vladimir |title=Symmetry |url=https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php/Symmetry |website=AoPS Online |publisher=Art of Problem Solving |access-date=14 April 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Van Fraassen |first1=Bas C. |title=Laws and symmetry |date=1989 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford ; New York |isbn=0-19-824860-1 |page=233}}</ref> however in Greek antiquity [[Ancient Greek mathematics|geometers]], while perhaps unconsciously using the principle of symmetry, would not have used such a phrase as the word symmetry ({{langx|grc|summetria}}) had the meaning of [[Commensurability (mathematics)|commensurability]].<ref name=Hon>{{cite book |last1=Hon |first1=Giora |last2=Goldstein |first2=Bernard R. |author2-link=Bernard R. Goldstein |title=[[From Summetria to Symmetry: The Making of a Revolutionary Scientific Concept]] |date=2008 |publisher=Springer Netherlands |location=Dordrecht |isbn=9781402084478 |url=<!--https://books.google.com/books?id=cVCCvN48MmIC&pg=PA70-->}}</ref>{{rp|pages=70–71}}

In 1945 [[George Pólya]] published ''[[How to solve it]]'' in which symmetry was one of the general strategies that could be used to solve problems.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Pólya |first1=George |title=How to solve it: a new aspect of mathematical method |date=2004 |orig-date=1945 |publisher=Princeton University Press |location=Princeton, N.J |isbn=978-0691119663 |edition=Expanded Princeton Science Library |url=https://archive.org/details/howtosolveit0000gpol_c0p2/page/198/mode/2up |url-access=registration |access-date=14 April 2026}}</ref>{{rp|pages=199–200}} In his later book ''Mathematical Discovery: On Understanding, Learning, and Teaching Problem Solving'' Pólya stated: "We expect that any symmetry found in the data and condition of the problem will be mirrored by the solution."<ref name=Discovery>{{cite book |last1=Pólya |first1=George |title=Mathematical discovery: on understanding, learning, and teaching problem solving |date=1981 |orig-date=1962 |publisher=Wiley |location=New York |isbn=0-471-08975-3 |edition=Combined |url=https://archive.org/details/bwb_W9-DFB-561/page/160/mode/2up |url-access=registration |access-date=14 April 2026}}</ref>{{rp|page=vol. 2, p. 161}}

[[TRIZ]] is a problem-solving methodology in the engineering field invented by [[Genrich Altshuller]] in 1946. TRIZ is based on 40 problem-solving principles, one of which is [[asymmetry]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Fogler |first1=H. Scott |last2=LeBlanc |first2=Steven E. |title=Strategies for creative problem solving |date=2008 |publisher=Prentice Hall |location=Upper Saddle River NJ |isbn=0-536-08783-0 |pages=127–133}}</ref> For example, changing the shape of an object from symmetrical to asymmetrical may solve the problem of users attempting to connect two components in the wrong way: the asymmetry forces the correct connection.<ref>{{cite web |title=TRIZ Principle No. 4: Asymmetry |url=https://www.triz40.com/TRIZ/Principle-04.php |publisher=SolidCreativity |access-date=17 April 2026}}</ref>
